verdict: Neither option on its own is the best choice. The evidence points to a staged hybrid. Step 1: remove alert noise first, as a precondition for any schedule change. Step 2: at the same time, open works council consultation, get labour-counsel advice on ArbZG s.3 and s.9-11, export timestamped page logs and audit runbook coverage per office. Step 3: only after the works council has agreed, run a time-boxed pilot of follow-the-sun 12-hour shifts, with Berlin on 07:00-19:00 Berlin time and SF on 10:00-22:00 PT. A pilot is itself a change to the Berlin on-call plan, so it cannot start before approval (E5, E15). Step 4: confirm the pilot or roll it back against criteria set in advance. Why: three alerts (disk-usage-warning-80pct, queue-lag-warning, cert-check-flap) produce 335 of 540 pages (about 62%) and only 2 of the 173 actions (E1, E2; K1-K5). Demoting them cuts load from about 6 to about 2.3 pages a day and keeps about 98.8% of actionable pages (K7, K8, K16). If pages are spread evenly, that is about 1.1 pages per 12-hour shift, which looks within the SRE benchmark of 2 incidents per shift (E6; K11). That fit is only indicative: the benchmark counts incidents, not pages, and comes from search snippets, and the unverified 58% night annotation suggests pages may cluster in one half of the day (E1, E3, E12). Tuning helps either option equally. So the schedule comparison is between option (a) with tuning and option (b) with tuning. The fair comparison is primary duty against primary duty. A secondary is paged only on escalation, and how often is unknown (E12). Follow-the-sun could also add a daytime secondary. On that basis, option (a) with tuning still leaves a 24/7 primary who, if pages are spread evenly, gets about 5.3 pages a week in their own local night (K33). Each engineer would average about 6.2 h a week of scheduled local-night primary duty (K39) and about 14.2 h a week of out-of-hours primary duty, assuming 09:00-17:00 weekday working hours (K30). For Berlin engineers on 24/7 weeks, the German night window (23:00-06:00) falls in the PT afternoon and evening, so PT afternoon and evening alerts trigger the 11-hour rest restart (E5, E13). Option (b) with tuning has no scheduled local-night duty, provided the incoming shift takes the handoff overlap (E9, E11, E16). Out-of-hours duty is about 9.8 h a week per SF engineer and 11 h per Berlin engineer (K26, K28), about 31% and 23% less than the option (a) primary figure (K37, K38). Weekend duty is about the same under both: about 5.3 h a week as an option (a) primary, against 4.8 h (SF) and 6 h (Berlin) under (b) (K34, K35, K40). So the decisive advantage of (b) is removing scheduled local-night duty, the stressor the survey names (E5). It is not a large cut in out-of-hours hours. The option (a) secondary adds further standby on top: about 28.4 combined out-of-hours standby hours a week per engineer (K31). Its real interruption load cannot be determined. The costs of option (b): Berlin carries about 12% more out-of-hours hours per person than SF, and 25% more total hours (K14, K29). Both sites are below the SRE benchmark of 6 engineers per site (E7). There are two handoffs a day, about 28 days a year of DST drift (E10; K22), and per-office skills coverage is unknown (E18). The Berlin shift avoids the statutory night window, but that does not settle every legal question. Call-out time counts as working time (E21), so call-outs on top of a normal working day, Saturday included, may exceed the s.3 daily ceiling of 8 h, extendable to 10 h (E23, unverified). Sunday and public-holiday call-outs fall under the s.9 ban. Saturday is a working day (Werktag) under s.3, not s.9. Sunday and holiday call-outs are most likely allowed for non-deferrable incident response under s.10(1) no.14, with a duty to record working time (E20). A substitute rest day may be due within 2 weeks after a Sunday call-out (E24, unverified). The floor of 15 work-free Sundays cannot bind, because each Berlin engineer would be on call about 13 weekends a year, leaving about 39 Sundays off call (K41). A collective agreement could change these rules, but whether one exists is unknown (E25). The same issues already apply to Berlin's 24/7 weeks under the current rotation and under option (a). Counsel must confirm them before the works council submission. How much night load follow-the-sun actually removes after tuning cannot be determined, because the CSV has no timestamps (E1, E3). Timestamped page logs would settle this.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Follow-the-sun with Berlin 07:00-19:00 and SF 10:00-22:00 PT is the only design in the evidence that removes scheduled local-night duty (22:00-06:00) for both offices. The incoming shift must take the handoff overlap; if it is added to the end of SF's shift, SF runs to 22:30. Option (a) keeps 24/7 weeks, so the primary still takes night pages, even after tuning: about 6.2 h a week of scheduled local-night primary duty per engineer on average. Noise removal cuts total interruptions by about 62% whichever schedule is chosen, so it does not separate the two options. Out-of-hours duty matters too, not just local night. Assume weekday working hours of 09:00-17:00. Average out-of-hours primary on-call duty per engineer per week would then be about 9.8 h (SF) and 11 h (Berlin) under follow-the-sun, against about 14.2 h under today's rotation or as option (a)'s primary, about 23-31% less. Weekend duty is about the same under both. Option (a)'s secondary adds standby on top (about 28.4 h combined), but a secondary is paged only on escalation and its paging rate is unknown. That combined figure is therefore not comparable with primary-only duty. How much of the tuning cut falls at night cannot be determined, because there are no timestamps.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Night interruptions = (pages that land in someone's local night) x (people exposed). Tuning reduces the first factor at every hour under any schedule. Option (a) leaves the share of pages in the primary's local night unchanged: with tuned load spread evenly, about 5.3 pages per primary week fall in 22:00-06:00 local (K33). It also adds a secondary who can be woken on escalation. Follow-the-sun moves coverage into each office's local day, so scheduled local-night exposure drops to zero by design. Out-of-hours exposure still remains: SF evenings 17:00-22:00, Berlin 07:00-09:00 and 17:00-19:00, and full 12-hour weekend days for both offices. So the out-of-hours saving over a 24/7 primary is moderate, and the weekend burden is roughly unchanged. If the 58% annotation is right (313.2 pages in 20:00-08:00 PT), at least 140 of those night-window pages were non-actionable, because only 173 pages were actionable at all.
strengths: With the overlap in the incoming shift, the E11 split puts neither office on scheduled duty in 22:00-06:00 local, and keeps Berlin out of 23:00-06:00 (E9, E11, E16)
Scheduled local-night primary duty drops from about 6.2 h a week per engineer (today and option (a)) to zero (K39; E11)

Out-of-hours primary on-call per person drops from about 14.2 h a week (today and option (a) primary) to 9.8 h (SF) or 11 h (Berlin), about 23-31% less (K26, K28, K30, K37, K38). This assumes 09:00-17:00 weekday working hours
Noise removal lowers interruptions at all hours and keeps 171 of 173 actionable pages (E2; K16)
Survey: 7 of 9 engineers name night pages as the main stressor (E5)
weaknesses: The 58% night share is unverified and there is no hour-of-day breakdown of actionable pages (E1, E3)
During the 8-hour-offset weeks, a split fixed to Berlin time pushes SF to 11:00-23:00 PT (E10, E11)
Option (a), even with tuning, still leaves about 5.3 local-night pages per primary week if pages are spread evenly (K33)

Follow-the-sun still includes 12-hour weekend shifts and weekday evenings or early mornings (K25, K27). Weekend duty per person (4.8-6 h a week) is about the same as for an option (a) primary (about 5.3 h) (K34, K35, K40)
The secondary's paging rate under option (a) is unknown, so its true burden cannot be set against follow-the-sun (E12)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Alert noise is the single biggest lever, and it applies equally to every schedule option. The three noise alerts produce 335 of 540 pages (62.0%) with 2 actions (0.6% actionable). The remaining four rows are 83.4% actionable. After demotion, load is about 2.3 pages a day, or about 1.1 per 12-hour shift if pages are spread evenly. That looks within the SRE benchmark of at most 2 incidents per 12-hour shift, and current load (about 3 per 12 hours) is above it. But the benchmark counts incidents, not pages, and uneven timing could push one half over it.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Cause-based or flapping warnings fire often but rarely need a human. SRE guidance is to page only on urgent, actionable, user-visible symptoms and to move cause signals to dashboards or tickets (E8). Removing them leaves the symptom alerts (api-5xx, db-replica-lag, payment-webhook) that drive real response. It also limits Sunday and holiday call-outs in Berlin to non-deferrable incidents, which is what the s.10(1) no.14 exception appears to cover (E20).
strengths: Arithmetic checked against the VERIFIED CSV: total 540, actionable 173, rate 32.0% (E1, E2; K1-K3)
Demotion loses only 2 of 173 actionable pages (E2; K16)
On an even spread, post-tuning load is below 2 per 12-hour shift (E6; K11)
weaknesses: queue-lag-warning did lead to 2 actions, so it needs replacing with a symptom-based alert, not just deleting (E2)
Per-day and per-shift figures assume pages are spread evenly. The 'other (14 alerts)' row cannot be broken down (E1, E2, E12)
The SRE benchmark counts incidents, not pages, and comes from search snippets only (E6)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Total on-call hours overstate the differences, because much of a 12-hour daytime shift overlaps normal work. Out-of-hours hours are the better fairness measure. Assume weekday working hours of 09:00-17:00 local. Follow-the-sun then gives each office's on-call person this much out-of-hours duty per week. SF: 5 h each weekday (17:00-22:00) plus 24 h at the weekend, 49 h in total. Berlin: 4 h each weekday (07:00-09:00 and 17:00-19:00) plus 24 h, 44 h in total. Per person that is about 9.8 h (SF) and 11 h (Berlin) a week, so Berlin carries about 12% more, less than the 25% gap in total hours. Weekend on-call is about 4.8 h a week per SF engineer and 6 h per Berlin engineer (about 13 weekends a year in Berlin). Under option (a), primary out-of-hours duty is shared evenly at about 14.2 h a week per person, including about 5.3 h of weekend duty. The secondary role adds standby on top (combined about 28.4 h out-of-hours and 10.7 h weekend), but its interruption load is unknown and probably much lower. So follow-the-sun lowers out-of-hours primary duty for both offices but gives no real weekend relief: Berlin's 6 h weekend figure is slightly above the 5.3 h under (a). Pay fairness cannot be assessed.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Splitting a fixed 168 h a week across unequal headcounts (4 vs 5) concentrates hours on the smaller office. Berlin's shift has fewer out-of-hours weekday hours (4 vs 5), which partly offsets this. If the unverified 58% figure is right, more pages could land in Berlin's 22:00-10:00 PT half, so Berlin's page burden per person could exceed the hours ratio. Weekend-day coverage counts the same for each office, so it is the main source of the Berlin imbalance (6 vs 4.8 h a week).
strengths: No office has scheduled local-night duty under the E11 split (E11)
The out-of-hours gap (about 12%) is smaller than the total-hours gap (25%) (K14, K29)
Option (a) is even across offices: about 14.2 primary out-of-hours hours per person per week, plus secondary standby of uncertain burden (K30, K31; E12)
weaknesses: Berlin carries more out-of-hours and weekend hours per person and possibly more pages (E12; K28, K29, K34)
Berlin's weekend duty under follow-the-sun (6 h a week) is slightly above an option (a) primary's (about 5.3 h) (K34, K40)
The 09:00-17:00 working-hours baseline is an assumption, not from the packet
The German allowance is unknown, so it cannot be compared with the US $400/week (E5, E17)

Berlin Sunday call-outs may require a substitute rest day within 2 weeks, which reduces Berlin capacity (E24, unverified). The floor of 15 work-free Sundays cannot bind: about 13 on-call weekends a year leave about 39 Sundays off call (K41)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Both options change the Berlin on-call plan, so both need works council agreement before anything changes, pilots included. The typical lead time is 4-8 weeks, and a deadlock goes to the conciliation board (Einigungsstelle). Follow-the-sun with Berlin on 07:00-19:00 keeps Berlin outside the statutory night window, which largely avoids the 11-hour rest restart. Under option (a), Berlin's statutory night (23:00-06:00) is 14:00-21:00 PT, which is PT afternoon and evening. Berlin primaries and secondaries on 24/7 weeks are therefore exposed to night call-outs and rest restarts. Avoiding the night window does not settle every legal question for the Berlin shift, however. Call-out time is working time (E21). On working days (Mon-Sat), call-outs on top of a normal 8-hour day could exceed the s.3 ceiling of 8 h, extendable to 10 h; this rests on background knowledge only (E23). Sunday and public-holiday call-outs are banned by default under s.9; Saturday is a working day under s.3, not s.9. Sunday and holiday call-outs are most likely allowed for non-deferrable incident response under s.10(1) no.14, and working time must be recorded (E20). If counsel disagrees, an authority authorisation under s.13 is a slower fallback (E22). A substitute rest day within 2 weeks after a Sunday call-out may be required (E24, unverified). The s.11 floor of 15 work-free Sundays cannot bind at about 13 on-call weekends a year per Berlin engineer (K41). A collective agreement could change these defaults, but whether one exists is unknown (E25). The same issues already affect Berlin's 24/7 weeks under the current rotation and under option (a), so they do not favour option (a). They do need to be settled in the works agreement.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Under BetrVG s.87(1) no.2, the works council co-determines working time, and on-call plans fall under this (E15). Under ArbZG s.5, a call-out generally restarts the full 11-hour rest (E13). Standby counts as rest, but call-out time counts as working time (E21). So the legal risk depends on call-out frequency and timing, which tuning reduces. With about 1.1 pages per 12-hour shift, the s.3 ceiling is less likely to be hit, but long incidents could still breach it (E23). One mitigation is a rule that call-out time on on-call working days replaces regular work.
strengths: The 07:00-19:00 Berlin shift avoids 23:00-06:00 entirely (E11, E16)
The HR notes and the secondary legal sources agree on the approval gate and the rest rule (E5, E13, E15)
For IT incident response there is a plausible statutory route for Sunday and holiday call-outs (E20)
weaknesses: The s.3, s.11 and s.7/s.12 points rest only on background knowledge; no statute texts were retrieved (E23, E24, E25)
Whether a trivial interruption restarts rest is disputed (E13 vs E14)
Whether Sunday standby without a call-out counts as Sunday employment is unresearched (E24)
An Einigungsstelle or an s.13 authorisation could push the timeline beyond 8 weeks (E15, E22)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Option (a) adds escalation depth and avoids handoffs, but keeps a 24/7 primary who is woken at night. Follow-the-sun adds two handoffs a day. It needs a written handoff, an overlap window in the incoming shift, a rule for the DST-drift boundary, holiday calendars for both offices, and confirmation that each office can handle every alert type alone, which is currently UNKNOWN. Both sites are below the SRE multi-site staffing benchmark of 6 per site, and Berlin is lowest at 4.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Handoffs create gaps in context, especially for incidents that span a boundary. Vendor guidance recommends a roughly 30-minute overlap and a mandatory structured handoff (E9). The PT-Berlin offset drops to 8 hours for about 28 days a year (E10). US and German public holidays differ, and Berlin holidays fall under the s.9 holiday ban (E9, E26).
strengths: After tuning, a shift carries about 1.1 pages on an even spread, leaving headroom for follow-up (E6; K11)
weaknesses: Per-office skills and runbook coverage is UNKNOWN (E18)
No empirical data on handoff-related incident risk (E9)
5 and 4 engineers per site is below the 6-per-site benchmark (E7)
The holiday calendars were not retrieved, and the weekend call-out load is not quantified (E26)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Noise removal is the cheapest, fastest and most reversible step. Option (a) adds a second person on paid standby every week. Its cost cannot be quantified, because no US secondary stipend is defined and the German allowance amount is unknown. Follow-the-sun needs works council approval (4-8 weeks or more), labour-counsel review of s.3 and s.9-11, scheduling tool changes, holiday calendars and a DST rule. If counsel finds Sunday and holiday call-outs fall outside s.10, an s.13 authorisation would add further lead time. It can be piloted and rolled back, but the rollback also touches the co-determined Berlin plan.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Cost scales with the number of people on paid standby and the allowance rates. Lead time is set by the works council gate and any authority authorisation. Reversibility depends on whether a change touches the co-determined plan.
strengths: Tuning can start immediately, in parallel with the works council consultation (E2, E15)
The legal review and the audit can run during the 4-8 week approval window (E5)
weaknesses: German allowance and US secondary stipend amounts are missing (E5, E17)
The works council position on a pilot is unknown (E15)
A possible s.13 authorisation adds lead time (E22)

claims.text: The CSV rows sum to 540 pages with 173 actionable, an actionable rate of about 32.0%.

disk-usage-warning-80pct, queue-lag-warning and cert-check-flap produce 335 pages (about 62.0% of all pages) with only 2 actions (about 0.6% actionable). The remaining 205 pages are about 83.4% actionable.

Demoting the three noise alerts would cut average load from about 6.0 to about 2.3 pages a day (about 15.9 a week; about 1.1 per 12-hour shift instead of 3, on an even spread). It would keep about 98.8% of actionable pages. This applies equally under either schedule option.

On an even spread, post-tuning load per 12-hour shift (about 1.1) is within the SRE benchmark of at most 2 incidents per 12-hour shift, and current load (about 3) exceeds it. The fit is indicative only. The benchmark counts incidents rather than pages and comes from search snippets, and uneven timing (for example, if the unverified 58% annotation holds) could put more load on one half.

With a 9-hour offset, a split of Berlin 07:00-19:00 and SF 10:00-22:00 PT leaves neither office on scheduled duty in 22:00-06:00 local time, and keeps Berlin outside the ArbZG night window of 23:00-06:00. This holds only if the incoming shift takes the 30-minute handoff overlap (Berlin from 06:30, SF from 09:30 PT). An overlap added to the end of SF's shift would run to 22:30 local. During the 8-hour-offset weeks the split cannot avoid both offices' nights: fixed to Berlin time, SF runs to 23:00 PT; fixed to PT, Berlin starts at 06:00.
The PT-Berlin offset is not a constant 9 hours. In 2026 it is 8 hours from 8-29 March and from 25 October to 1 November, about 28 days in total.

Under follow-the-sun, each office covers 84 h a week: about 16.8 h per SF engineer against 21 h per Berlin engineer, about 25% more per Berlin person and more than today's average of about 18.7 h. These are total hours, much of which overlaps normal working hours. CL18 gives the out-of-hours comparison.

Option (a) puts each engineer on call (primary or secondary) about 2 weeks in 9 (about 22.2% of weeks, about 37.3 h a week of combined standby on average), with 24/7 night exposure unchanged. How often the secondary is actually paged is unknown.

Any change to the Berlin on-call plan, whether a secondary role, 12-hour shifts or a time-boxed pilot of either, needs works council agreement before it takes effect. HR reports a typical lead time of 4-8 weeks, and a deadlock goes to the Einigungsstelle.

In Berlin, a night call-out generally restarts the full 11-hour rest period. Designs that keep Berlin off night duty therefore avoid lost next-day capacity. Whether trivial interruptions count is disputed.

The claim that 58% of pages fired between 20:00 and 08:00 PT cannot be verified. The CSV has no timestamps, and 58% of 540 is 313.2, not a whole number. The night share of actionable pages cannot be determined.

If the 58% annotation is correct, at least about 140 of the roughly 313 night-window pages were non-actionable, because only 173 pages in total were actionable. Noise removal would then necessarily remove some night pages. The exact share remains unknown.
Whether both offices can handle every alert type independently, which follow-the-sun requires, cannot be determined from the evidence.
Pay fairness and the cost of adding a secondary cannot be determined. The German collective allowance amount and any US secondary stipend are not specified.
Both sites (5 SF, 4 Berlin) are below the SRE multi-site benchmark of at least 6 engineers per site, which is a sustainability risk for follow-the-sun, especially in Berlin.
Burnout is unlikely to come from rotation structure alone. Night exposure (structure) and noise (volume) are separate contributors, and noise makes up about 62% of pages.
With raw load of about 42 pages per 24/7 week, if the 58% annotation is correct, about 24.4 of them would fall in 20:00-08:00 PT. Under option (a) these land in an SF primary's local night.

Assume weekday working hours of 09:00-17:00 local. Average out-of-hours on-call duty per engineer per week as primary (or sole on-call) would then be about 9.8 h (SF) and 11 h (Berlin) under follow-the-sun, with Berlin about 12% higher. It would be about 14.2 h under today's rotation and for option (a)'s primary, so follow-the-sun is about 23-31% lower like for like. Weekend on-call duty averages about 4.8 h a week per SF engineer and 6 h per Berlin engineer under follow-the-sun, against about 5.3 h as an option (a) primary, which is roughly the same. Option (a)'s secondary adds standby on top: about 28.4 h out-of-hours and 10.7 h weekend in combined primary and secondary standby. A secondary is paged only on escalation, at an unknown rate, so these combined figures overstate its interruption burden and are not a like-for-like comparison with follow-the-sun.

Option (a) with tuning still leaves the 24/7 primary about 5.3 pages a week in their own local night (22:00-06:00), if tuned pages are spread evenly. Each engineer would average about 6.2 h a week of scheduled local-night primary duty. Combined primary and secondary local-night standby is about 12.4 h, but the secondary's paging rate is unknown. Follow-the-sun with tuning has no scheduled local-night duty.

Under ArbZG s.9, Sunday and holiday call-outs by Berlin engineers are banned by default. They are most likely allowed for non-deferrable incident response on production systems under s.10(1) no.14, with call-out working time recorded. Standby itself counts as rest; only call-out time counts as working time. Saturday is a working day (Werktag), so Saturday call-outs fall under the s.3 daily limits rather than s.9.

The evidence cannot settle several questions. Whether call-outs on working days (Mon-Sat) during a Berlin on-call shift breach the ArbZG s.3 daily maximum (8 h, extendable to 10 h). Whether s.11 requires a substitute rest day within 2 weeks after a Sunday call-out, and whether Sunday standby without a call-out counts as a worked Sunday. Whether a collective agreement under s.7/s.12 changes these defaults for the Berlin entity. These points rest only on background knowledge or are UNKNOWN, and need labour counsel. They apply to Berlin's 24/7 weeks under every option, not only to follow-the-sun.

One option (a) variant has a secondary in the other office take the primary's local-night pages. That amounts to follow-the-sun with weekly cross-office pairs: its night coverage, works council requirement and handoff needs are the same. Because each pair needs one person from each office, Berlin engineers would be on duty about 1 week in 4 and SF engineers about 1 week in 5.

If the s.11 rule of at least 15 work-free Sundays a year applies (unverified), it cannot bind under the proposed rotation. Each Berlin engineer is on call about 13 weekends a year, leaving about 39 Sundays off call even if every on-call Sunday counted as worked. Only the substitute-rest-day rule is a real capacity factor.

alternatives.option: Option (a): weekly 24/7 primary plus a secondary, with no noise tuning
alternatives.comparison: It keeps about 42 pages a week on a 24/7 primary (K20) and does not remove local-night duty (E11). Each person's on-call share doubles to about 2 weeks in 9 (K19). The primary role alone carries about 14.2 out-of-hours hours a week on average, and the secondary adds standby with an unknown paging rate (K30, K31; E12). It adds a second paid standby person each week, at a cost that cannot be quantified (E5, E17). For Berlin weeks, PT afternoon and evening alerts fall in Berlin's statutory night and trigger rest restarts (E13). It scores worst on C1 and C4 and best only on avoiding handoffs (C5).

It gets the same tuning benefit as the hybrid: about 15.9 pages a week, about 2.3 a day (K8, K9). But the 24/7 primary still receives about 5.3 local-night pages a week if pages are spread evenly (K33). Compared like for like (primary duty only), engineers average about 6.2 h a week of scheduled local-night duty and about 14.2 h of out-of-hours duty (K30, K39). Under (b) with tuning the figures are zero and 9.8-11 h, about 23-31% less out of hours (K26, K28, K37, K38). Weekend primary duty is similar (about 5.3 h against 4.8-6 h; K34, K35, K40). The secondary adds standby on top, but its interruption burden is unknown (E12). Berlin 24/7 weeks keep the rest-restart risk (E13) and the same s.3 and s.9 questions (E20, E23). It is better than (b) on handoffs and on hours parity between offices. On the stated stressor, night pages (E5), it is worse.

alternatives.option: Option (a) variant: weekly cross-office pair, where the secondary in the other office takes the primary's local-night pages
alternatives.comparison: This answers C1 without formal 12-hour shifts. In practice it is follow-the-sun with weekly pairs. The Berlin partner covers SF nights (22:00-06:00 PT is about 07:00-15:00 Berlin at a 9-hour offset). The SF partner covers Berlin nights (23:00-06:00 Berlin is 14:00-21:00 PT). Each pair needs one person from each office, so Berlin frequency is about 1 week in 4 against 1 in 5 for SF (E4, E12), the same imbalance as (b). It still needs works council approval (E15), routing handoffs and the per-office skills check (E18). It is a reasonable way to frame (b) to the team, not a separate solution.

alternatives.option: Option (b): follow-the-sun 12-hour shifts, with no noise tuning
alternatives.comparison: It removes scheduled local-night duty (E11), but each shift carries about 3 pages, above the 2-per-12h benchmark (E6; K10). Berlin takes about 25% more total hours and about 12% more out-of-hours hours (K14, K29). More call-outs also make the s.3 daily-maximum and Sunday-work questions more pressing for Berlin (E20, E23).

alternatives.option: Noise removal only, keeping the current weekly 24/7 primary
alternatives.comparison: Fastest and cheapest. Load drops to about 15.9 pages a week (K9), and the schedule itself needs no change or approval (E15). But the primary still gets about 5.3 local-night pages a week on an even spread (K33), and Berlin primaries still face night call-outs (E11, E13). Load still falls on one person all week, with about 14.2 out-of-hours hours a week on average (K30). This is a credible fallback if the works council, legal review or skills audit blocks follow-the-sun.

alternatives.option: Recommended hybrid: noise removal first, then, after works council approval, a follow-the-sun pilot (Berlin 07:00-19:00, SF 10:00-22:00 PT) with structured handoffs
alternatives.comparison: Compared with option (a) with tuning, it trades handoff risk and a Berlin hours imbalance (K29) for no scheduled local-night duty (K39) and about 23-31% less out-of-hours primary duty per person (K26, K28, K30, K37, K38). Weekend load is about unchanged (K34, K35, K40). It requires works council agreement before the pilot (E15), a per-office runbook audit (E18), a DST rule (E10), holiday calendars (E26), and counsel confirmation of the s.3 and s.9-11 points (E20, E23-E25).

tradeoffs: Night relief against hours fairness: follow-the-sun removes scheduled nights but gives each Berlin engineer about 12% more out-of-hours on-call than each SF engineer, and 25% more total hours (E12; K14, K29).

Escalation depth against exposure: a secondary adds backup but doubles each person's on-call weeks and adds a second paid standby. Its cost cannot be quantified without stipend and allowance figures (E5, E12, E17; K19).
Fewer handoffs against fatigue: weekly 24/7 avoids two daily handoffs but keeps one person exposed around the clock, even after tuning (E9, E11; K33).
Speed against durability: noise removal is quick and reversible, while schedule changes are gated by the works council for 4-8 weeks or longer (E5, E15).
Aggressive demotion against hidden incidents: queue-lag-warning had 2 real actions, so deleting it outright risks missing them (E2).
edgeCasesAndFailureModes: DST mismatch weeks (8-29 March, 25 October to 1 November 2026): a boundary fixed to Berlin time moves SF to 11:00-23:00 PT, and one fixed to PT moves Berlin to 06:00-18:00. Pick one rule in advance and tell both offices (E10, E11).

Handoff overlap placement: if the 30-minute overlap is added to the outgoing SF shift, SF runs to 22:30, or 23:30 in mismatch weeks if boundaries are fixed to Berlin time. Put the overlap in the incoming shift (E9, E11).
Incidents that span the 19:00 Berlin / 10:00 PT boundary: without an overlap window and a written handoff, context is lost (E9).
A Berlin call-out that runs late into the 19:00 boundary pushes the next-day start back under the 11-hour rule (E11, E13).

A Berlin engineer works a full 8-hour working day (Mon-Sat) and then handles more than about 2 h of call-outs. The day may exceed the s.3 ceiling (unverified), so call-out time should replace regular work on on-call days (E21, E23).

Sunday and Berlin public-holiday call-outs (for example 8 March) fall under the s.9 ban; Saturday call-outs are working-day work under s.3. Sunday and holiday call-outs need the s.10(1) no.14 exception, recorded working time and possibly a substitute rest day within 2 weeks. The floor of 15 work-free Sundays cannot bind at about 13 on-call weekends a year (E20, E23, E24, E26; K41).
Absence or attrition at a site with 4 engineers puts more load on the remaining 3 (E7).
Demoted alerts turn into real incidents, for example disk fill or certificate expiry. Symptom-based or deadline-based replacements and ticket routing are needed (E2, E8).
If timestamps show that actionable pages cluster in the Berlin half or near boundaries, the fairness and reliability picture changes (E3, E12).
Even a brief night acknowledgement by a Berlin engineer may restart rest under the strict view (E13, E14).

counterarguments.argument: Option (a) is safer because a secondary adds escalation depth and avoids handoff risk.
counterarguments.response: Compared fairly, with tuning applied to both, option (a) avoids handoffs and keeps hours equal between offices. But its primary still gets about 5.3 local-night pages a week on an even spread (K33), with about 6.2 h a week of scheduled local-night primary duty per engineer against zero under follow-the-sun (K39). That leaves the stated stressor, night pages, largely in place (E5). On out-of-hours primary duty the gap is moderate (about 14.2 h against 9.8-11 h, K26, K28, K30), and weekend load is about the same (K34, K35, K40). So the case against (a) rests mainly on night exposure, not on total out-of-hours hours. The evidence does not show a need for more escalation depth at about 2.3 pages a day (K8). If depth is wanted, a daytime secondary can be added within follow-the-sun. Handoff risk can be reduced with an overlap and written handoffs (E9).

counterarguments.argument: Once noise is removed, a schedule change may not be needed at all.
counterarguments.response: Possibly. That is why tuning comes first and the schedule change is measured in a pilot. But real actionable alerts would still wake a 24/7 primary at night (K33), and Berlin primaries would still face rest-restart call-outs (E11, E13). Whether residual night load is material cannot be determined without timestamps (E3).

counterarguments.argument: Follow-the-sun is unfair to Berlin, which has fewer people.
counterarguments.response: Correct, though less so than total hours suggest. Berlin carries about 11 vs 9.8 out-of-hours hours a week per person, about 12% more (K28, K26, K29), and 6 vs 4.8 weekend hours (K34, K35). In return, Berlin avoids all scheduled statutory night duty and rest restarts (E11, E16). Possible mitigations: compensate 12-hour shifts under the collective policy (amount unknown, E17), have SF take some weekend shifts, or rely on tuned load to keep each shift light. These belong in the works council negotiation.

counterarguments.argument: Berlin weekend and holiday coverage under follow-the-sun breaks the Sunday-work ban, so follow-the-sun is unlawful.
counterarguments.response: Not obviously. Sunday and holiday work is banned by default (s.9). Saturday is a working day and falls under the s.3 daily limits instead. Maintaining computer systems appears to fall under the s.10(1) no.14 exception for non-deferrable incidents. Working time must be recorded, and an s.13 authorisation is a fallback (E20, E22). Standby itself is rest time (E21). Berlin 24/7 weeks under option (a) or today's rotation face the same question, so it is not a point against (b) specifically. Counsel must confirm (E23-E25).

counterarguments.argument: The 58% night figure shows most load is at night, so the schedule is the root cause.
counterarguments.response: The figure is an unverified annotation (E1, E3). Even if accurate, at least about 140 of those night pages were non-actionable (K18), so noise is also a large share of the night problem (E19).

counterarguments.argument: Short night acknowledgements do not interrupt rest under German law, so option (a) is fine for Berlin.
counterarguments.response: That is a contested minority view from 2012-era commentary (E14). The mainstream secondary sources say a call-out restarts the full 11 hours (E13). A design should not depend on the contested view. Labour counsel should confirm.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The only options are (a) weekly 24/7 plus a secondary or (b) follow-the-sun 12-hour shifts.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Alert-noise removal is a stronger first lever than either schedule, and it applies to both. It removes about 62% of pages while keeping 171 of 173 actionable ones. With tuning applied to both, follow-the-sun removes scheduled local-night duty and option (a) does not. The evidence supports a hybrid: tune first, then follow-the-sun after works council approval.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: 58% of pages fired between 20:00 and 08:00 US Pacific time.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Unverified. It is a free-text annotation with no timestamps, and 58% of 540 is 313.2, not a whole number. Treat it as an estimate until raw logs are supplied.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The CSV total of 540 pages is correct and the 'other' row is complete.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: The total is confirmed: the rows sum to 540, with 173 actionable. Whether the combined 'other (14 alerts)' row is complete cannot be checked.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: Burnout is caused mainly by the rotation structure.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Structure and noise are separate contributors. About 62% of pages are near-zero-action noise, so fixing the structure alone would leave most of the volume in place.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The PT/CET offset is a constant 9 hours.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: It is 8 hours for about 28 days a year (8-29 March and 25 October to 1 November in 2026), so shift boundaries need a DST rule.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: Both offices can handle every alert type independently.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Unknown. There is no evidence on per-office skills, ownership or runbook coverage, so this must be audited before follow-the-sun goes live.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The HR notes accurately reflect ArbZG and BetrVG.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Broadly consistent with secondary legal sources, but incomplete. A deadlock goes to the Einigungsstelle, which can take longer than 4-8 weeks. Whether trivial interruptions restart rest is disputed. The notes also leave out the Sunday and holiday ban (s.9) and its IT exception (s.10(1) no.14), which comes with a duty to record working time. Further rules may apply: the daily maximum on working days, Mon-Sat (s.3), substitute rest days after Sunday work (s.11), and collective-agreement deviations (s.7/s.12). These rest on background knowledge only. Statute texts were not retrieved, so this needs counsel confirmation.

practicalImplications: Rollout step 1 (weeks 0-4): demote disk-usage-warning-80pct to a ticket or dashboard, with a separate symptom or fill-rate page if needed. Fix the flapping in cert-check-flap and replace it with an expiry-deadline alert. Review the 2 actionable queue-lag-warning cases and replace that alert with a user-visible symptom alert (E2, E8). Ask HR whether these monitoring changes need works council involvement, since BetrVG s.87(1) no.6 was not researched (E15).

Rollout step 2 (start in week 0, in parallel): export raw timestamped page logs and measure the hour-of-day and weekend split of actionable pages before and after tuning. This settles the 58% question, the Berlin page share and the expected weekend call-out load (E3).

Rollout step 3 (start in week 0): before the works council submission, get labour-counsel confirmation of four points. First, that Sunday and holiday call-outs fall under ArbZG s.10(1) no.14, and how call-out time will be recorded (E20). Second, whether s.3 daily maximums require reduced regular hours on Berlin on-call working days (Mon-Sat), or a rule that call-out time replaces regular work (E21, E23). Third, whether s.11 substitute rest days apply after Sunday call-outs, and whether Sunday standby alone counts as Sunday work (E24). Fourth, whether a collective agreement with s.7/s.12 opening clauses covers the Berlin entity (E25). Then open the works council consultation on a time-boxed follow-the-sun pilot. Cover Berlin 07:00-19:00, the DST boundary rule, handoff overlap placement, weekend and holiday rules, the 12-hour shift allowance under the collective policy, and rollback terms. Plan for 4-8 weeks plus the risk of an Einigungsstelle, or an s.13 authorisation if counsel requires one (E5, E15, E17, E22).
Rollout step 4 (weeks 2-6): audit runbook, access and service-ownership coverage per office for every paging alert. Close the gaps through pairing and shadow shifts before the pilot (E18).

Rollout step 5 (only after works council approval): pilot follow-the-sun for a fixed period. Use a 30-minute overlap taken by the incoming shift (Berlin from 06:30, SF from 09:30 PT), a mandatory written handoff in a fixed channel, and one DST rule chosen in advance. Load both offices' public-holiday calendars into the scheduling tool, and consider SF covering German holidays and some weekend shifts to offset Berlin's extra hours (E9, E10, E11, E12, E26).

Rollout step 6: set success and rollback criteria in advance. For example: local-night pages per person at or near zero; pages per shift below 2; no missed or late acknowledgements on api-5xx, db-replica-lag or payment-webhook alerts; no s.3 or rest-period breaches in the Berlin working-time records; and a repeat burnout pulse survey. Roll back to the tuned weekly rotation if the criteria fail (E5, E6, E20).
Do not adopt option (a) as the main fix. If a secondary is wanted for depth, make it a daytime, same-office backup within follow-the-sun, and only if pilot data shows a need (E11, E13).
remainingUncertainty: The hour-of-day and weekend distribution of all pages and of actionable pages is unknown, and the 58% figure is unverified (E3).
Per-office skills, ownership and runbook coverage are unknown (E18).
The German collective on-call allowance and any US secondary stipend are not specified, so pay fairness and the cost of a secondary cannot be quantified (E5, E17).

Legal points rest on search snippets or background knowledge. The statute texts were not retrieved, the trivial-interruption question is disputed (E13, E14, E15, E16), and the s.3, s.11 and s.7/s.12 points are unverified (E23, E24, E25).
Whether Sunday standby without a call-out counts as Sunday employment, and whether the Berlin entity has a collective agreement with opening clauses, are unknown (E24, E25).
The out-of-hours figures (K25-K31, K37-K40) assume 09:00-17:00 weekday working hours in both offices. That assumption is not in the packet.

How often an option (a) secondary would actually be paged is unknown (E12). The combined standby figures (K31, K32, K36) therefore cannot be converted into an interruption burden, and the like-for-like comparison uses primary duty only.
The SRE benchmarks (2 incidents per 12-hour shift, 6 per site) come from search snippets, count incidents rather than pages, and assume Google-scale services (E6, E7).
Whether led_to_human_action was recorded reliably, and whether the 'other (14 alerts)' row hides further noise, is unknown (E1, E2).
Boundary-crossing incident handling and handoff-related incident risk have no empirical evidence (E9).
furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion: Timestamped page logs. If actionable pages cluster in PT daytime, at weekends or near the boundaries, the night benefit, the benchmark fit or the fairness picture changes.

Escalation data from comparable rotations, or a trial of a secondary role. These would show the true burden and benefit of an option (a) secondary, and whether a daytime secondary within follow-the-sun closes any reliability gap.
A per-office runbook and access audit. Large gaps could make follow-the-sun infeasible in the near term, favouring tuning plus the current weekly rotation.
The works council position. A refusal, or conditions such as limits on Berlin shift frequency or weekend duty, could block or reshape the pilot.

Labour-counsel confirmation of ArbZG s.3, s.9-11 and s.5 (including the Bagatelle view), and of any collective agreement under s.7/s.12. A restrictive reading of Sunday and holiday call-outs could force SF to cover those days, or require an s.13 authorisation.
The actual German allowance and the US secondary stipend amounts, which could change the cost and fairness ranking.
Post-tuning page volume measured over 2-4 weeks. If residual night load is negligible, a schedule change may be unnecessary.
